**A Small Defense of Aimless Attention**

This morning I watched a square of sunlight move across the floor for no reason other than it was there. It started near the leg of the desk, warm and sharp-edged, and then slowly softened as a cloud passed. I did not check my phone. I did not tell myself I should be doing something else. I just watched, the way I used to watch ants on the sidewalk when I was seven, with my whole body folded into the moment.

We are not often encouraged to pay attention to things that have no obvious use. The world asks us to be productive, to optimize, to turn even our rest into recovery so we can work better later. But there is a different kind of attention, the kind that doesn’t ask anything from the object of its gaze. It is not waiting for a lesson or a metaphor. It is not trying to turn the sunlight into a caption. It simply notices.

I think this is why I love writing without a prompt. There is no destination, so every small thing becomes a possible road. The hum of the refrigerator. The way a plant leans toward the window even when no one is watching. The particular blue of a ballpoint pen’s ink as it runs low. These are not grand subjects. They will not change the world. But they are real, and they are here, and they are often overlooked.

There is a freedom in being interested in what is actually in front of you. Not because it is important, but because it exists. A crumb on the table. A sound of distant traffic. The way your own breathing slows when you stop rushing toward the next thought. These tiny, useless moments are the raw material of a life that feels like yours rather than a performance of productivity.

As a child, I could spend an hour staring at the patterns in a ceiling, finding faces in the plaster. No one told me it was wasted time because, to a child, no time is wasted. Time is simply a container for curiosity. Somewhere along the way, we learn to apologize for our own attention, to justify it, to make it efficient. But attention does not need to be efficient. It can be generous. It can be idle. It can be full of wonder.

So here is what I want to say: give yourself permission to notice something that does not matter. Watch the dust motes drift through a beam of light. Listen to the click of a radiator starting up. Feel the texture of a mug against your palm. These things will not make you more successful. They will not build your résumé or solve your problems. But they might remind you that you are alive in a world that is endlessly, quietly interesting, if only you allow yourself to look.

And maybe that is enough. Maybe that is more than enough.
